newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil up, traders warn OPEC on cheating.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil up, traders warn OPEC on cheating.

text.p: World oil markets surged late on Wednesday after shuffling sideways earlier, after OPEC oil ministers agreed in Vienna to freeze their production quotas for six months.

On London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), benchmark Brent futures for August closed a hefty 34 cents a barrel up at $18.21, a little off from a session high of $18.45 on the back of the OPEC news.
In New York, NYMEX's WTI August futures ended the day 52 cents up at $19.55 a barrel.
OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman said shortly earlier in Vienna that the producer group had agreed to freeze its 25.03 million barrels per day ceiling until the end of the year.
He said that OPEC members agreed to go back on their allocations but added no threats were made to overproducers -- led by Venezuela.
Some oil market traders said the statements from the OPEC meeting were ambiguous and that some market players were doubtful that the violators would stick to the agreement.
"Who's to say that Venezuela that has broken its quota in the past will stick to it," one IPE trader said.
Earlier on Wednesday, senior oil traders said they saw a chance of more price falls if OPEC failed to plug some of the leaks in its much abused quota system.
Prices have already dropped 25 percent this year to $18 a barrel.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) is currently pumping some 2 million barrels per day (bpd) above it's self imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
Even some elegates at the Vienna meeting doubted the pressure on Venezuela would have much impact.

"OPEC is going to become important again in the future but they must act now to stop the cheating," said Bob Finch heading of trading at Vitol SA in London, the world's largest independent oil trader and refiner.
A failure to address overproduction at this meeting will "almost certainly hit prices" he said.
Iraq said it expects to resume exporting oil under a U.N. oil-for-food pact early July, ending three weeks of uncertainty which had helped buoy sagging crude prices.
Under the terms of the accord implemented last December, Iraq is permitted $2.14 billion worth of oil over 180 days to raise money for food and medicine.

Iraqi exports during the first phase of the deal averaged 660,000 bpd -- equivalent to the output of OPEC minnow Qatar -- but could increase exports to around 740,000 bpd when the second phase starts.
If oil prices fall further, export flows from Iraq could rise and put more pressure on the market, said traders.
Brimming oil tanks are already beginning to weigh on prices for next winter.

In Europe and the United States, winter heating oil stocks are about 20 percent and 13 percent above year ago levels. And traders say the summer gasoline season in the West stalled at the starting line.
Even a large slug of unexpected oil demand from Nigeria this week failed to help prices.
But despite a bearish mood among many traders there are signs of better demand ahead.
Oil demand in Asia, eastern Europe, Latin America and China is booming and helping to offset more sluggish demand in Western industrialised nations.
